screens.media_alt: Dr. Omar, a family physician, presenting the clinic's purpose, mission and goal.
screens.body_html:
Purpose — helping people live longer, healthier, happier lives

Mission — the world's most customer-centric healthcare company

Goal — outstanding patient experience + excellent clinical outcomes
screens.narration_text: OMAR: Our purpose is simple to say and hard to do: we help people live longer, healthier, happier lives, including people who are well today. Our mission is to be the world's most customer-centric healthcare company. In practice, every role asks one question: did this help the patient? Our goal follows from that: outstanding patient experience, alongside excellent clinical outcomes. Honestly, my first week here, I felt there was too much to take in. You don't need to remember everything today — just where to find it.

screens.title: Our four values
screens.prompt_html: Values are behaviours. Open each one and look for something you already do.

tabs.label: Collaborative
tabs.body_html:
Unites diverse

Act together · Treat everyone with respect · Be transparent · Embrace diverse perspectives · Deliver outstanding results

tabs.label: Responsible
tabs.body_html:
Creating a culture of accountability

Own our decisions and actions · Make things happen · Demonstrate high professional standards · Hold yourself and each other accountable

tabs.label: Ambitious
tabs.body_html:
Set new standards

Go above and beyond · Make new possibilities happen · Challenge the status quo · Become industry shapers · Deliver outstanding results

tabs.label: Caring
tabs.body_html:
Putting empathy first

Act with empathy · Everyone matters · Love our customers · Deliver with quality

screens.narration_text: OMAR: Every clinic has values on a wall. Ours only matter if you can see them in what people do. Collaborative: we act together, treat everyone with respect, and stay transparent. Responsible: own your decisions, make things happen, and hold each other to the same standard. Ambitious: go above and beyond, and challenge the status quo when it stops serving patients. Caring: act with empathy, because everyone matters. As you go on, think which of these you already do without being asked.

screens.title: Values in action
screens.prompt_html: Six things people did this week. Match each one to the value behind it.

pairs.left_html: You admit a scheduling mistake to your manager and fix it.
You ask a colleague in another department for their view before you decide.
You stay with an anxious patient until the nurse arrives.
You suggest a faster way to book follow-up appointments.
You share the reason for a delay with the team instead of staying quiet.
You check your own work against the professional standard before you sign it off.

feedback.correct_html: Right. Notice that Responsible and Collaborative each appear twice: the values overlap in real work, and one action can show more than one.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not all six. Read each action again and ask what the person was actually choosing to do — own it, involve others, reach further, or care for someone.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: Here are six things people did this week. Match each one to the value behind it.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: Strategy feels like someone else's job until you find your own work inside it. Here are the seven pillars. Closer: convenient access — clinics, community clinics and home health care, digital services, telemedicine. Cure: the best Saudi doctors, clinical outcomes, centres of excellence, prevention and wellbeing. Capabilities: a repeatable model for running and growing clinics, with real governance. Culture: our mission and values, servant leadership, a culture of excellence. Clinicians: a caring environment, competitive benefits, room to grow. Care: seamless experience, empathy, loyalty built through My Care. Cost: competitive cost to serve. Whichever one you picked, that's your line in.

screens.title: Which pillar?
screens.prompt_html: My Care follow-up calls that build patient loyalty support which pillar?

options.feedback_html: Care. My Care follow-up calls are named in the Care pillar under “build loyalty through My Care”. Loyalty is a service and relationship outcome, not an access outcome.
Closer covers access: physical, community and home health care, digital services, and the call centre and telemedicine. A phone call is access; a follow-up call that builds loyalty is Care.
Culture is mission, values and servant leadership. It shapes how we behave, not this service.
Cost is about cost to serve: revenue cycle, efficiency and overhead. Loyalty work sits on the service side.

feedback.correct_html: Care. My Care follow-up calls are named in the Care pillar under “build loyalty through My Care”. Loyalty is a service and relationship outcome, not an access outcome.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Closer is about access — physical, community, digital and telemedicine. Culture is mission, values and leadership. Cost is efficiency. The pillar that names My Care and loyalty is Care.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: One to try. My Care follow-up calls build patient loyalty. Which pillar do they belong to?

screens.narration_text: OMAR: Who do we serve? First, patients and their families — sick or healthy. Many of the people who walk in today are well, and we want them to stay that way. Second, the community around each clinic. Third, corporates and insurers. Three groups, one standard.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: We opened our first clinic in North Jeddah in 2017. In 2019 we started the employment check-up unit, our first corporate service. Then came East Jeddah, the dental centre, and Petro-Rabigh in 2023, our first clinic inside a corporate community. Riyadh followed in 2024, a flagship to put the brand on the map. The last two years added our first community clinics. Nine years, nine steps, one idea: bring good care closer.

screens.title: Our code of ethics
screens.body_html:
Respect — uphold the rights, privacy and dignity of patients, families and colleagues.

Integrity — transparent practice; disclose any potential conflict of interest.

Accountability — a culture that encourages reporting safety concerns and adherence to policy.

Innovation & collaboration — support research and community engagement to improve quality and outcomes.

Ethical dilemma? Incident report within 24 hours + ethics team. Pending B14 / D8.
screens.narration_text: OMAR: Four values sit under everything. Respect — the rights, privacy and dignity of patients, families and colleagues. Integrity — be transparent, and disclose any conflict of interest. Accountability — a culture where people report safety concerns instead of staying quiet. Innovation and collaboration — research and community work that improves outcomes. And the rule you'll use: faced with an ethical dilemma, complete an incident report within twenty-four hours and bring in the ethics team. You're never expected to work it out alone.
screens.media_alt: Four icons for Respect, Integrity, Accountability, and Innovation and collaboration.

screens.title: A supplier you know
screens.notes: Companion: Noor, L5 avatar 56 px with 3 px #652D8C ring and label 'Noor · Safety liaison' above each situation card: char-noor-avatar-neutral; after a choice the feedback line shows char-noor-avatar-happy (best choice) or char-noor-avatar-concern (other choices). Never beside the choice buttons.
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-noor-avatar-neutral}}Noor · Safety liaison

Three moments, three decisions. Nobody is watching.

nodes.prompt_html: You're on a panel evaluating three suppliers for a clinic fit-out. One bidder is your cousin's company. The evaluation starts in an hour.
nodes.image_alt: A small meeting room where a supplier evaluation is being discussed.

choices.text_html: Say nothing — you can score their bid fairly.
choices.feedback_html: Even a fair score looks compromised. Integrity means disclosing a potential conflict of interest before the work starts, in procurement as much as in recruitment.

choices.text_html: Declare the conflict in writing to the panel chair and step back from scoring that bid.
choices.feedback_html: Right. You disclose the potential conflict and remove yourself from the decision. Nobody has to guess afterwards, including you.

choices.text_html: Step out of the meeting quietly and say nothing.
choices.feedback_html: Leaving is better than scoring, but silence doesn't help: the panel still doesn't know why, and the conflict stays undocumented. Declare it, then step back.

nodes.prompt_html: A colleague from another department asks you to “help” a patient skip the queue, and offers you a gift.
nodes.image_alt: A clinic corridor with a reception desk and two patients waiting.

choices.text_html: Decline, and explain that access to care is not something we trade.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Fair access is part of Respect — every patient in that queue is waiting for the same reason. A gift makes it a transaction.

choices.text_html: Do it once, then return the gift.
choices.feedback_html: Returning the gift afterwards doesn't undo it. Someone else waited longer because of a favour, and the gift makes it a transaction.

choices.text_html: Ask the patient to wait outside and slot them in when it's quiet.
choices.feedback_html: Quiet or not, that patient is still moving ahead of people who waited. Decline, and say why.

nodes.prompt_html: A week later you're not sure whether something you saw counts as an ethical issue. Nobody else has raised it.
nodes.image_alt: A desk with a laptop open on an incident report form.

choices.text_html: Wait until you're certain before involving anyone.
choices.feedback_html: Waiting is the common mistake. The policy doesn't ask you to be certain; it asks you to act on the dilemma you have.

choices.text_html: Raise it with a colleague or the committee, and complete an incident report within 24 hours so the ethics team can advise.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Consult colleagues for anything beyond your expertise, and complete an incident report within twenty-four hours so the ethics team can guide you. That's Accountability working.

choices.text_html: Mention it informally to your line manager and leave it there.
choices.feedback_html: A quiet word is a start, but it leaves no record and no route to advice. Report it within twenty-four hours and bring the ethics team in.

feedback.correct_html: Three out of three. You declared the conflict, you held the line on queue-jumping, and you used the reporting route instead of guessing. That is Integrity and Accountability as behaviour, not as a poster.
feedback.incorrect_html: Below three. The pattern to hold on to: disclose a conflict early, never trade access for a favour, and when you genuinely don't know, report it within twenty-four hours and ask the ethics team.

screens.narration_text: NOOR: Three moments now, and nobody is watching. First: you're on a panel evaluating suppliers for a clinic fit-out, and one bidder is your cousin's company. The evaluation starts in an hour. What do you do?

screens.title: Rights or responsibilities?
screens.prompt_html: Nine statements from the notice in reception. Sort them into the right column.

items.text_html: Access to care regardless of race, gender or disability
Information and informed consent before treatment
Refuse treatment after understanding the risks
Ask for a patient advocacy representative
Follow the treatment plan and attend appointments

feedback.correct_html: Right. Six rights and three responsibilities. The full notice is posted in the reception area if you ever need to point someone to it.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. A right is what the patient can expect from us. A responsibility is what we ask of them so that we can look after them safely. Look again at the three that ask the patient to do something.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: Nine statements from reception. Sort each: is it what the patient can expect, or what we ask of them?

screens.title: She said no
screens.prompt_html: A patient refuses a blood test after the doctor has explained the risks. What is the right response?

options.text_html: Respect the refusal, check she understood the risks, document it, and tell the doctor
options.feedback_html: Right. Refusal of treatment is a patient right once the risks are understood. Your job is to check understanding, document the refusal, and inform the doctor.

options.text_html: Ask the clinic manager to persuade her to agree
options.feedback_html: Bringing in a manager to talk her round turns a right into pressure. She can refuse once she understands the risks.

options.text_html: Take the sample anyway, because the doctor ordered it
options.feedback_html: Proceeding against a competent patient's refusal is not consent. Stop and escalate to the doctor instead.

options.text_html: Ask a family member to consent instead
options.feedback_html: A family member cannot replace her consent. Only she can decide, once she understands the risks.

feedback.correct_html: Right. Refusal of treatment is a patient right once the risks are understood. Your job is to check understanding, document the refusal, and inform the doctor.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not that one. A competent patient can refuse after the risks have been explained. Persuasion, proceeding anyway, or substituting a family member's consent all override a right.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: Last one here. A patient refuses a blood test after the doctor has explained the risks. What do you do?

screens.title: Leave at a glance
screens.prompt_html: Nine types. Open the one you need — the full tables are in the Quick Reference.

items.title: Annual
items.body_html: After probation, with your line manager's approval. Carry over up to 5 days; use them by end of March (consulting-room physicians: end of June). Pending B9.

items.title: Sick
items.body_html: Tell your line manager. Valid medical report required. First 30 days full pay; days 31–90 pending B1; days 91–120 unpaid.

items.title: Work injury
items.body_html: Covers work hours and commuting. Report to your line manager and HR the same day or the next day.

items.title: Maternity
items.body_html: 12 weeks. You may start up to 4 weeks before the expected delivery date.

items.title: Exam
items.body_html: Paid, for academic exams only. Actual exam days only. Documents at least 2 weeks in advance. IELTS, TOEFL and similar are not eligible.

items.title: Scientific
items.body_html: Paid days per profession each year, for academic exams. Needs the MD's pre-approval. Cannot be carried over. Pending B10.

items.title: Hajj
items.body_html: Muslim employees with two full years of service. 10–15 days including Eid. Hajj permit copy required. Pending B11.

items.title: Compassionate
items.body_html: Marriage 5 days · paternity 3 · immediate relative 5 · sibling 3 · death of a husband pending B2.

items.title: Official holidays
items.body_html: Eid al-Fitr 4 days · Eid al-Adha 4 days · Founding Day 22 February · National Day 23 September.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: Nine types. Open the ones you need. Annual: after probation, five days carried over, used by end of March. Sick: valid report needed. First thirty days paid in full. Work injury covers commuting, and has a same-day or next-day deadline. Maternity: twelve weeks, starting up to four weeks early. Exam leave: academic exams only, documents two weeks ahead. Scientific: by profession, and can't be carried over. Hajj: two years' service and a permit. Compassionate: marriage, paternity, bereavement. Then Eid, Founding Day, National Day. We'll practise the four people ask about most.

screens.title: How many days?
screens.prompt_html: Four grades, four entitlements. Match each grade to its annual leave, in working days. Entitlement pending B9.

feedback.correct_html: Right. Entitlement rises with grade: 30, 27, 25 and 22 working days. Your contract and the Quick Reference both show your own grade.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. The entitlement rises with grade, from 22 working days at grades A to E up to 30 at grade H. Match them again.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: Four grades, four entitlements. Match each grade to its annual leave, in working days.

screens.title: Forty days of sick leave
screens.notes: Companion: Dr. Omar char-omar-thinking, L3 right column half-body 320-380 px, clear of the ledger; below 768 px he drops under the ledger. Alt: 'Dr. Omar, a family physician, thinking through the example.'
screens.intro_html: A colleague is off sick for 40 days in one year, with valid medical reports from My Clinic. How is the pay worked out?

steps.action_html: Days 1–30 — tell your line manager you are unwell.
steps.rationale_html: Notification is the first requirement. Sick leave is accepted only with a valid medical report, and your manager needs to know today, not at the end of it.
The first thirty days of valid sick leave in a year are paid in full.

steps.action_html: Days 31–40 — reduced pay. Per the slide as written: 25% deducted, so 75% of salary. Pending B1.
steps.rationale_html: The second band cuts pay by a quarter. Continuous and separated periods count the same way, so the band follows the total days in the year, not one absence.
The bands run 1–30, 31–90 and 91–120. Forty days never reaches this band, but it's the ceiling you should know.

steps.action_html: Check the report: from outside My Clinic, it needs Staff Health Clinic approval.
steps.rationale_html: Reports from My Clinic are accepted as they are. Anything from another provider has to be approved, or the leave isn't valid.

screens.self_explanation_prompt_html: What changes if the medical report comes from another hospital?
screens.narration_text: OMAR: One example, properly. A colleague is off sick forty days in a year, with valid reports. First, she tells her line manager — that's first, not last. The first thirty days are paid in full. Ten days fall into the next band, and that's where pay drops. Note the detail people miss: it's the total in the year that sets the band, not one spell. Beyond ninety days it's unpaid. And if the report is from outside My Clinic, the Staff Health Clinic must approve it. Now: what changes if her report comes from another hospital?

screens.title: The leave desk
screens.notes: Companion: Noor char-noor-avatar-neutral, L5 avatar 56 px with 3 px #652D8C ring and label 'Noor · Safety liaison' above each request card; never beside the choice buttons. Alt: 'Noor, the safety liaison, hosting the leave desk.'
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-noor-avatar-neutral}}Noor · Safety liaison

Four colleagues, four questions. You're the one they've asked.

nodes.prompt_html: Yousuf is a lab technician. He asks for two days of scientific leave, and he already has the MD's pre-approval for his documents. How many days can he take this year?
nodes.image_alt: An HR service desk with a laptop and two chairs.

choices.text_html: Two days — that's the technician allowance, and unused days can't be carried over.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Scientific leave is 2 days a year for lab and radiology technicians, 3 for nurses, 4 for pharmacists, 5 for other physicians and dentists, and 7 for consultants. It also can't be carried over.

choices.text_html: Seven days — that's the allowance.
choices.feedback_html: Seven days is the consultants' allowance. Technicians get two. The allowance follows the profession, not the request.

choices.text_html: None — scientific leave is only for consultants and physicians.
choices.feedback_html: Not so. Every profession in the table has an allowance; technicians have the smallest, at two days a year.

choices.text_html: Two days now, and he can carry the rest into next year.
choices.feedback_html: The days are right, the carry-over isn't. Scientific leave cannot be carried over — unused days are lost.

nodes.prompt_html: Amal is a nurse. She asks for exam leave to sit IELTS next month, and she has her documents ready.
nodes.image_alt: An HR service desk with a laptop and two chairs.

choices.text_html: Refuse: IELTS is not an academic examination, and it's named as not eligible.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Exam leave is paid leave for academic examinations only, and IELTS, TOEFL and Microsoft certifications are named as not eligible. Having the documents ready doesn't change eligibility.

choices.text_html: Approve it — she has her documents in on time.
choices.feedback_html: Documents matter, but eligibility comes first. IELTS is not an academic examination and is named as not eligible.

choices.text_html: Approve half the exam days as a goodwill gesture.
choices.feedback_html: Well meant, but the rule is about the type of exam, not the number of days. IELTS is not eligible, so there are no days to approve.

nodes.prompt_html: Reem is a pharmacist with one full year of service. She asks for Hajj leave and has her Hajj permit ready.
nodes.image_alt: An HR service desk with a laptop and two chairs.

choices.text_html: Not yet — Hajj leave needs two full years of continuous service.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Two full years of continuous service is the eligibility rule, and one year doesn't meet it. The permit is needed, but it doesn't shorten the service requirement.

choices.text_html: Yes — one year of service is enough.
choices.feedback_html: It isn't. Hajj leave is for Muslim employees with two full years of continuous service.

choices.text_html: Yes, now that she has the Hajj permit.
choices.feedback_html: The permit is a requirement, not a substitute. Without two full years of service she isn't eligible, permit or not.

nodes.prompt_html: Sara is a receptionist. She slipped on the way into work this morning and her ankle is painful. What does she need to do?
nodes.image_alt: An HR service desk with a laptop and two chairs.

choices.text_html: Tell her line manager and HR today or tomorrow — commuting is covered as a work injury.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Work injury covers commuting as well as work hours, and the deadline is the same day or the following day. HR then reports the case to GOSI.

choices.text_html: Wait and see whether she needs time off before reporting it.
choices.feedback_html: Waiting is the mistake this rule exists to prevent. The report has to go to her line manager and HR the same day or the next day, whether or not she ends up taking time off.

choices.text_html: Tell her commuting accidents aren't covered.
choices.feedback_html: They are. Work injury applies during work hours and while commuting to and from work, for Saudi and expatriate employees alike.

feedback.correct_html: Three or four. You checked eligibility before you answered, which is the whole job at this desk: type of leave, who qualifies, and what document is missing.
feedback.incorrect_html: Fewer than three. The habit to build is to check three things every time — the type of leave, the eligibility rule, and the document. Two of these four turned on eligibility, not on paperwork.

screens.narration_text: NOOR: Now you're on the other side of the desk. Four colleagues, four questions. First: Yousuf, a lab technician, wants scientific leave and already has the MD's pre-approval.

screens.title: Leave rules: quick practice
screens.prompt_html: Answer until the practice says you're ready. It stops early if you've got it.

items.prompt_html: How many unused annual leave days can you carry over?
items.explain_html: Carry-over is capped at 5 days. Anything above that is lost at the end of the carry-over window.
items.scaffold_html: The cap is a small number — single digits.

items.prompt_html: Carried-over annual leave must be used by when?
items.explain_html: Carried-over leave has to be used by the end of March of the following year.
items.scaffold_html: It's the end of a spring month.

items.prompt_html: A consulting-room physician carries over leave. By when must it be used?
items.explain_html: Consulting-room physicians have a later deadline: the end of June.
items.scaffold_html: This group gets three months more than everyone else.
It's measured in weeks, not months — and it's the longest of the three options.

options.text_html: Up to 2 weeks before the due date
Up to 4 weeks before the due date

items.explain_html: You may start up to 4 weeks before the expected delivery date.
items.scaffold_html: The allowance is measured in weeks before the due date.

items.prompt_html: Exam leave documents must be submitted how far in advance?

options.text_html: On the day of the exam

items.explain_html: Documents — the exam schedule and course schedule, plus a result transcript afterwards — must go in at least two weeks in advance.
items.scaffold_html: Think in weeks, and it's more than one.

items.prompt_html: How many days of leave for your own marriage?
items.scaffold_html: Marriage attracts the same number of days as bereavement of an immediate relative.
It's the same number as bereavement of a sibling.

items.prompt_html: Bereavement leave for the death of a sibling?
items.explain_html: Death of a sibling is 3 calendar days. Death of an immediate relative — spouse, parent or child — is 5.
items.scaffold_html: Immediate relatives attract more days than siblings.

items.prompt_html: How many days is each Eid holiday?
items.explain_html: Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha are each 4 days.
Founding Day is 22 February. National Day is 23 September — the two are easy to swap.
items.scaffold_html: It's a February date, and the other national holiday falls in September.

items.prompt_html: Can unused scientific leave be carried over?
items.explain_html: Scientific leave cannot be carried over. It also needs the MD's pre-approval, but approval doesn't create a carry-over.
items.scaffold_html: Approval and carry-over are two different rules; only one of them is mentioned in the source.

feedback.correct_html: You've got the leave numbers. Carry-over, maternity, compassionate and the holidays are the four people ask about most — they're all in the Quick Reference.
feedback.incorrect_html: Leave numbers are worth a second look in the HR Quick Reference. The ones people mix up are the carry-over deadline, Founding Day versus National Day, and sibling versus immediate-relative bereavement.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: A short practice set now. It adapts: if you're getting these, it will finish early. If you're not, it'll keep going for a few more.

screens.title: What GOSI is
screens.body_html:
GOSI — General Organization for Social Insurance.

Saudi employees only, until retirement at 60.

9.75% you + 11.75% My Clinic = 21.5% of basic + housing. Rates pending B12.
screens.media_alt: GOSI contribution: the employee pays 9.75%, My Clinic pays 11.75%, a total of 21.5%.
screens.narration_text: OMAR: GOSI is the General Organization for Social Insurance — the government body for social protection in Saudi Arabia. It applies to Saudi employees, until retirement at sixty. The split matters: you pay nine point seven five per cent of basic plus housing. My Clinic pays eleven point seven five. So the real contribution is twenty-one point five, and most of it isn't yours.

screens.title: Working out 585 riyals
screens.intro_html: Basic 4,800 + housing 1,200. What is the monthly GOSI deduction from your salary? Rates pending B12.

steps.rationale_html: GOSI is charged on basic salary plus housing allowance, not on basic alone and not on total pay with allowances and bonuses.
Only your share is deducted from your salary. The company's 11.75% is paid on top and never appears as a deduction on your payslip.
6,000 × 0.0975 = 585. This is the line you'll see on your payslip.
steps.artifact_caption: Your 9.75% employee share (585 SAR) sits alongside My Clinic's 11.75% contribution.

screens.self_explanation_prompt_html: Which part of the salary is the percentage applied to?
screens.narration_text: OMAR: Let's do one together. Basic four thousand eight hundred, housing one thousand two hundred. Add them — GOSI is charged on basic plus housing, so six thousand. Apply your rate, nine point seven five per cent. The company's rate never touches your payslip. Six thousand times nought point nought nine seven five is five hundred and eighty-five riyals a month. That's the line to look for.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.prompt_html: Basic 6,000 + housing 1,500. Your monthly GOSI deduction = ___ SAR. Rates pending B12.

feedback.correct_html: Right. Basic 6,000 + housing 1,500 = 7,500, and 7,500 × 9.75% = 731.25 SAR a month.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Add basic and housing first — that's 7,500 — then take 9.75% of that, not of the basic alone.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: Your turn. Basic six thousand, housing one thousand five hundred. What's your monthly GOSI deduction?

screens.title: Working out overtime
screens.intro_html: Basic 6,000. What is your overtime rate on a normal working day, and on a public holiday? Eligibility by grade pending B3.

steps.rationale_html: The formula uses a 30-day month at 8 hours a day, so 240 hours. Everything else in the calculation hangs off this one number.
steps.artifact_caption: Hourly rate = basic salary ÷ 30 days ÷ 8 hours, then multiplied by 1.5 (regular) or 2.0 (public holiday).

steps.rationale_html: Overtime on a normal working day is paid at time and a half.
Overtime on a public holiday is paid at double time. Note it's the same hourly rate — only the multiplier changes.

screens.self_explanation_prompt_html: Why is the hourly rate worked out from 240 hours, not 208?
screens.narration_text: OMAR: One caveat before the numbers: whether you're eligible for overtime at all depends on your grade. Check that first. Now the arithmetic. Basic six thousand. Divide by thirty days times eight hours — two hundred and forty hours — and you get twenty-five riyals an hour. On a normal working day, multiply by one and a half. That's thirty-seven riyals fifty. On a public holiday, multiply by two. Fifty riyals an hour. Same hourly rate both times. Only the multiplier moves.

screens.title: Four hours on Tuesday
screens.prompt_html: Basic 6,000. You work 4 overtime hours on a normal working day. What is the overtime pay?

options.feedback_html: Right. Hourly rate is 6,000 ÷ 240 = 25, then 25 × 1.5 × 4 hours = 150 SAR.
That's 25 × 4. You've worked out the plain hourly pay and left out the time-and-a-half multiplier.
That's 25 × 2 × 4. Double time is for a public holiday, not a normal working day.
That doesn't come from the formula. Go back to the hourly rate first: 6,000 ÷ 240.

feedback.correct_html: Right. Hourly rate is 6,000 ÷ 240 = 25, then 25 × 1.5 × 4 hours = 150 SAR.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Build it in three moves: 6,000 ÷ 240 = 25 an hour, × 1.5 for a normal day, × 4 hours.

screens.narration_text: OMAR: One for you. Basic six thousand. You work four overtime hours on a normal working day. What's the overtime pay?

steps.hint_html: Look for Add Leaves under Time and Absences.

Not every step. The route is always the same: sign in, then Time and Absences, then Add Leaves. The last two steps are the form itself.

screens.title: If you ever leave
screens.body_html:
Accept your contract on Qiwa.

Resign in Oracle.

Notice: 2 months, honoured by both parties.

EOS + experience certificate within 15 days of your last working day.
screens.narration_text: OMAR: Two ends of one story. Starting: you accept your contract on Qiwa, the Ministry of Human Resources platform. Leaving: a resignation is a request, so it goes through Oracle. Notice is two months, and it runs both ways. End-of-service benefits and your experience certificate follow within fifteen days of your last day.
screens.media_alt: Four steps: Qiwa contract, Oracle resignation, two months notice, and end-of-service settlement within 15 days.

screens.title: Three weeks' notice
screens.prompt_html: You accept a new job starting in 3 weeks. What happens with your notice?

options.text_html: You must serve the contractual 2 months unless My Clinic agrees otherwise; submit the resignation in Oracle
options.feedback_html: Right. The notice period is two months and it binds both sides, unless My Clinic agrees to something different. And a resignation is a request, so it goes in through Oracle.

options.text_html: You can leave in 3 weeks — a new job overrides the notice period
options.feedback_html: A new job doesn't override the contract. The two months stands unless My Clinic agrees to shorten it.

options.text_html: Email your manager; Oracle is only for leave requests
options.feedback_html: Oracle isn't only for leave. Resignation, letters and certificates are all service requests, and they need a record.

options.text_html: Give one month: notice is shorter for grades A to E
options.feedback_html: The notice period in your contract isn't set by grade in this policy. Assume two months unless your contract says otherwise.

feedback.correct_html: Right. The notice period is two months and it binds both sides, unless My Clinic agrees to something different. And a resignation is a request, so it goes in through Oracle.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not that one. The contractual notice is two months, and it binds both sides. You can always ask HR whether they'll agree to less, but you can't assume it.

sections.title: Values & strategy
sections.advice_html: Revisit the four values and the 7C pillars. The one to remember: Care is where My Care and patient loyalty sit.

sections.title: Ethics & patients' rights
sections.advice_html: Disclose conflicts early, never trade access to care, and when you're unsure, report within 24 hours. A right is what the patient can expect; a responsibility is what we ask of them.

sections.title: Leave
sections.advice_html: Check three things on every request: the type of leave, the eligibility rule, and the document. The tables are in the HR Quick Reference.

sections.title: Pay & social insurance
sections.advice_html: GOSI is basic plus housing × 9.75%. Overtime is basic ÷ 240, then × 1.5, or × 2 on a public holiday.

sections.title: Systems & licences
sections.advice_html: Requests go through Oracle. Contracts on Qiwa, licences on Mumaris, guides on the intranet. Renew your licence well before it expires.

sections.title: ID, dress code & contracts
sections.advice_html: Front office wears the uniform, the medical team wears scrubs and a coat, back office is business attire. Notice is two months both ways.
